To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) state-of-the-art deep convolutional networks for classification easily fit a random label of the training data; (2) this phenomenon is qualititatively unaffected by regularization; (3) this phenomenon occurs even if we use random noise instead of real images as inputs to the network; (4) this phenomenon can occur even for depth two networks; and (5) this phenomenon occurs for networks that are over-parameterized in the sense that their number of parameters exceeds their number of data

(i) large neural networks are overparameterized, (ii) overparameterization allows them to fit a random labeling, (iii) this phenomenon is qualitively unaffected by regularization, (iv) this phenomenon occurs even when the training data are unstructured random noise, (v) this phenomenon occurs in depth two neural networks, and (vi) the phenomenon occurs even when training is done with stochastic gradient descent.

1) state of the art neural networks trained with stochastic gradient descent easily fit a random labelling of the training data, 2) this phenomenon occurs even if we substitute true images by random noise, 3) this phenomenon is unaffected by explicit regularization techniques, and 4) this phenomenon can be explained theoretically by the expressivity of depth two networks with a number of parameters greater than the number of data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how deep neural networks can generalize from a finite number of examples.
the question: why do large random neural networks generalize well?
the question: “What does it mean for a model to generalize well?” and we conclude that common understanding within complex models is incomplete and needs to be revisited.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the generalization ability of deep networks is a consequence of the vast amount of knowledge that is encoded in the prior distribution over neural network parameters, and not a consequence of a special property of the model architecture.
current deep learning models are not able to generalize well.
the generalization performance of deep networks is still a mystery.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
our experiments show that the success of deep learning in practice cannot be simply explained by traditional models.
deep nets easily fit the random labels, and this phenomenon occurs because of the vast capacity of deep nets, despite the regularization methods employed.
deep networks easily overfit the training data, but despite this strong ability to fit complex function, they still generalize well
The main takeaway from our work is that
state of the-art convolutional networks fit random data on par with true data.

state of the-art convolutional networks fit randomized training labels better than we expected, and that more study is needed to understand why they perform well despite this apparently poor behavior.
neural networks succeed, not because they are robust to overfitting, but rather because they are especially bad at it.
